claims.text: Discovery runs in one direction: from what the business needs to how you would measure it. Starting from a solution, such as "let's build an agent," skips the facts that decide whether it will work.
claims.checked_by: Studio author: drafted from the cited source text; no verbatim excerpt recorded; SME verification pending

claims.text: Business outcome: what changes for the business, and who owns that result. Use case: the actor and the job they need to do. Workflow: how the job is done today, with its steps, handoffs, and systems. Data: the information the job needs, where it lives, and who can access it. Success metrics: the evidence that the outcome improved.

claims.text: If you start with a complex agent design, you lock in assumptions before you know the data or the workflow. Following the chain exposes missing facts and dependencies, such as an unowned knowledge base or a permission model nobody has checked, while the design can still change. An agent idea is one possible implementation. It is never the starting requirement.

claims.text: Good questions produce evidence: real examples, frequency, the people affected, and consequences. Weak questions produce opinions.

claims.text: "Walk me through the last time this happened" gets far more useful detail than "Is search painful?" Follow up with: Where did the information live? Who else was involved? How did you decide the answer was trustworthy? How often does this happen, and how long does it take? What happens when it goes wrong? Glean's partner question bank covers four areas: strategic goals and current success metrics, the day in the life of key personas, pain points and workarounds, and what "good" looks like 6 to 12 months out.

claims.text: "Walk me through what happens from when a case arrives to when you send the answer. Where do you search, and what access do you need?" "How often does this happen each day, how long does it take, and how many agents do it?" "Who tracks how quickly and how well cases are resolved, and in which system?" The first exposes effort, meaning the systems and permissions involved. The second exposes reach and volume. The third finds the metric owner and the source of proof.

claims.text: Impact is more than how many people a use case touches. It combines reach, frequency, and the business consequence: cost, revenue, risk, or quality.
claims.checked_by: Studio author: drafted from the cited source text; no verbatim excerpt recorded; SME verification pending

claims.text: Reach: the affected users. Frequency: how often the event occurs. Consequence: what happens to cost, revenue, risk, or quality when it goes well or badly. A workflow used by 200 people twice a day may be a bigger capacity opportunity than a weekly task for five people. But a rare compliance event can still matter a great deal. Record the rationale rather than forcing every impact into a seat count.

claims.text: High, medium, and low ratings are useful in a workshop, but each needs a short rationale and an evidence status. "High, because about 200 agents do this several times a day (champion's estimate, to confirm with the ticketing data)" is defensible. "High" on its own is not.

claims.text: Treating addressable users as active users. Not everyone who could use a capability will. Double-counting. The same saved minutes can't be claimed twice under two benefit lines. Monetizing too early. Use financial modeling only after the assumptions are explicit and labeled.

claims.text: Glean's value-selling training notes that most use cases deliver multiple value drivers. A complete customer view, for example, can improve both growth and efficiency. Mapping those connections makes a stronger narrative and speaks to several stakeholders at once. It also raises the risk of double counting, so state which driver each number belongs to. claims.text: Compare two use cases: a broad, low-friction policy lookup used by most employees, and a rare, high-risk approval process in finance.
claims.checked_by: Studio author: drafted from the cited source text; no verbatim excerpt recorded; SME verification pending

claims.text: Policy lookup: record the population and frequency, such as "most employees, a few times a month" (to confirm), and the time per lookup. Impact is mainly capacity and experience. Approval process: record its severity and controls, such as what an error costs and which controls apply. Impact is mainly risk, and seat count understates it. Discuss value and feasibility separately for each. Leave unsupported monetary claims unquantified until the inputs are confirmed.

claims.text: Effort is where optimistic use cases fail. A simple-sounding request can depend on several systems, complex permissions, or actions that require security review. Surface these risks in discovery, not after a demo.
claims.checked_by: Studio author: drafted from the cited source text; no verbatim excerpt recorded; SME verification pending

claims.text: Glean's partner enablement lists technical gotchas to surface in discovery: Data and connectors | The source of truth is unclear; no native connector; immature or rate-limited APIs; on-premises systems | "Where is the canonical record, and which system wins on conflicts?" Data footprint | A small-sounding use case needs legacy systems, archives, or large files | "How much history does this need?" Permissions and identity | Row- or field-level permissions; multiple directories; shared mailboxes; exceptions | "Who can see what, and are there exceptions?" Structured expectations | Expecting exact
claims.checked_by: Fact Integrity Auditor (studio spot check)

claims.text: Validate feasibility with the people who own the systems. Don't infer it from a use case description. Also consider change management. A technically easy use case still takes effort if it changes how a team works. Boundary Don't claim that generic retrieval will perform deterministic joins, or that an agent can write to any system. Verify current capabilities with the Glean account team, and get owner commitments before rating a use case as easy.
claims.checked_by: Studio author: drafted from the cited source text; no verbatim excerpt recorded; SME verification pending

claims.text: Effort hides in the data. Ask system owners about these areas before you rank a use case as low effort. Connectors Is there a clear source of truth and a connector? Permissions Row- or field-level rules; multiple identities Structured data Exact joins and aggregations expected Freshness Real-time needs versus periodic indexing Write-backs Which systems may the agent update? Data quality Labels, ownership, and tribal knowledge
claims.checked_by: Studio author: drafted from the cited source text; no verbatim excerpt recorded; SME verification pending

claims.text: A use case calls for an agent that reads five systems and updates a CRM record after each customer call. Identify at least four effort risks.
claims.checked_by: Studio author: drafted from the cited source text; no verbatim excerpt recorded; SME verification pending

claims.text: Connector availability for all five systems, and whether each source is canonical. Identity and permissions: whether users see only the records they're entitled to. Data consistency across systems, such as conflicting account names or fields. An approved write-action model: what is written, and the audit trail, idempotency, and handling of partial failures. Security review of write actions into the CRM. Mark each as unresolved and assign a validation owner before rating effort.
claims.checked_by: Studio author: drafted from the cited source text; no verbatim excerpt recorded; SME verification pending

claims.text: A simple matrix is usually enough for live alignment. Glean's Value Playbook also provides an eight-dimension scoring model that covers factors such as business value potential, measurability, time to value, and cross-functional applicability. This can help expose differences between close candidates. Caution The playbook's scoring model rates some complexity dimensions so that a higher score is better. Interpret those dimensions carefully before adding scores together. Don't turn the raw total into an automated feasibility gate. This course uses explicit rationale and human review.
